Q: Are GCS Object Lifecycle Management Delete actions billed as Class A operations? A:

In the billing page, you can see that the life cycle delete operation is free of charge.
No hidden cost.
If you use soft delete, you will continue to pay the object storage cost for the soft deletion duration. If you do not restore the object, you do not pay for Class A operation (you pay for 1 Class A operation for 1000 object restore in bulk restore mode. See the billing page too:
"In buckets that use soft delete, one Class A Standard storage operation is charged per 1,000 objects processed as part of a bulk restore operation, rounded up so that at least one Class A operation is always billed. This is in addition to the operations charge assessed per object restored.")

Q: Interpolation of quaternion orientations and vector positions A:

I followed the same principal idea of the Roman Kolesnikov's solution, but arrived at a slightly different expression.

We start by computing the relative rotation

qr = ~q1 * q2

and decompose it into axis a and angle α representation.

Then, v = a x (p2 - p1) gives us a vector v in the plane of the rotation that lies exactly at the half angle between our two end points pointing towards the center. Using the point (p1 + p2) / 2 we can go along v until we arrive at the center. However, the correct length of the vector is 0.5*|p2-p1|/(tan(0.5*α))! I tested this by transforming points on the unit circle and checking them agains the known solution.

Putting things together, the correct solution for the rotation center is

c = (p1 + p2)/2 + (a x (p2 - p1)) * (0.5 / tan(0.5*α))

Note that the norm of vector |p2 - p1| is already contained in the length of the cross product under the assumption that the axis a has unit length. By construction a and (p2 - p1) are orthogonal such that the sinus between the two is always 1. I.e. |a x (p2 - p1)| = |p2-p1|.

For the final interpolation of both position and quaternion with parameter t, I constructed a new quaternion qt from a and t*α and

qfinal = q1 * qt

prot = qt * (p1 - c) * ~qt + c

prot is still not the final position. While the point has the right amount of rotation around c, it does not move in the direction perpendicular to the rotation plane. We can add this and obtain:

pfinal = prot + ⟨a, p2-p1⟩ * t * a

Q: CSS best practises and when to use each A:

Typically, for Web topics, some of the best tutorials can be found here: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS.

As much as I can tell, your entire approach is wrong. The tutorials usually don't tell you much about when to use one technique or another. You simply don't need it. They are more about how the techniques affect your result, in this case, rendering and dynamic behavior. And even you don't have to think about it. The logic is the opposite: first, you learn some representative part of the techniques and understand how they work. You should not take them a kitchen recipe. When you come to understanding, you take a practical problem, decide what rendering you want to achieve, and then think logically about what CSS rules can help. You decide. You should not be very goal-oriented; that is, you should try any effect you find curious to see.

As you can see, the question “when to use each” goes out of the equation.

Q: Applying a specific condition for a total in python A:

You can use enumerate() to iterate over a list and also keep track of the list position:

for position, book in enumerate(booklist):
    if position == 0:
        # this is the first book
        # apply special price
    else:
        # this is not the first book
        # apply regular price
